h1: How much cash to keep in reserve before a brewpub opens
title: Cash Reserve Before a Brewpub Opens | Craft Beer School
desc: How much cash a brewpub should hold in reserve before opening: months of fixed costs, licensing delays and the slow first quarter.
teaser: Brewpubs rarely fail on the day they open. They fail three months later, when the reserve runs out.
standfirst: Founders put most of their money into the build and keep too little for the months after opening. Those months are when sales are lowest and surprises are highest. Here is how to size the reserve and where it goes.
sections: The reserve pays for the gap between opening and break-even

On opening day you have a finished brewpub and fixed costs that start immediately: rent, salaries, utilities, loan repayments, insurance and licence fees. Sales take time to build. Most brewpubs need several months before monthly sales cover monthly costs. Some need longer.

The reserve is cash set aside to cover that gap. It is separate from capex and from build contingency. If you spend it on the bar top or an extra fermenter, it is gone when you need it most.
Start with three to six months of fixed costs

A common rule of thumb is to hold three to six months of fixed operating costs in reserve at opening. Where you land in that range depends on how sure you are of your opening date and of early sales.

A worked example for a mid-sized brewpub in a metro, with round numbers:

  • Rent and maintenance charges: ₹6 lakh a month.
  • Salaries for brewing, kitchen, floor and management: ₹9 lakh.
  • Utilities: ₹2.5 lakh.
  • Loan repayments: ₹3 lakh.
  • Insurance, software, accounting and other fixed costs: ₹1.5 lakh.

Fixed costs come to ₹22 lakh a month. Four months of cover is ₹88 lakh. That sounds like a lot, because it is. Founders who budget ₹20 lakh of working capital for a place costing ₹22 lakh a month to run are relying on full houses from week one.
Licensing delays eat the reserve before you open

In many Indian cities the final licences come late, sometimes weeks after the fit-out is complete. Every month between handover and first sale costs rent, salaries for staff already hired and loan interest, with no revenue at all.

Build that risk into the reserve. If your plan assumes opening in month eight after signing the lease, ask what happens if it is month ten. Two extra months of rent and core salaries can be a large share of your reserve. Rules and timelines vary by state, so ask a licensing consultant how long approvals are taking now, not two years ago.
The first beer is not on tap on day one

A brewpub cannot sell its own beer until the first batches are brewed, fermented and conditioned. A clean lager can need four weeks or more from brew day to glass. Ales are faster, often two to three weeks.

That means ingredients, CO2, cleaning chemicals and brewing staff costs start well before beer sales do. Plan trial brews too: the first batches on a new brewhouse are often used to dial in the system. Some may not be good enough to sell. Our guide to planning the opening month sets out the timeline.

Opening week is busy with friends, family and the curious. The weeks after are the real test. A forecast that assumes 70% of capacity from month one is a wish. One that ramps from 30% in month one to 60% by month four is easier to defend.

Build the forecast from covers and spend per head, not from total revenue. Our guide to forecasting beer volumes before opening shows how. Then check the reserve against the low case, not the base case. If the reserve only works in the good case, it is too small.
Keep the reserve where you can reach it

Hold the reserve in a separate bank account or a sweep deposit you can draw on within a day. Do not lock it into a fixed deposit with heavy penalties or lend it to the build. Agree in advance with your partners what triggers a draw and what needs everyone's approval.

An overdraft or working capital limit arranged with your bank before opening is a useful backstop. It is much harder to arrange when you are already short.

Review the reserve every week for the first three months. Write down the balance, the week's sales against forecast and the weeks of cover left at current burn. When cover drops below eight weeks, act: cut hours on quiet days, delay hiring, push events and bookings. A reserve that is watched lasts far longer than one that is simply spent.

The reserve is the part of the plan that keeps a good brewpub alive long enough to prove itself. Getting the number right means a real forecast, a real cost base and an honest low case, which is the work we do with founders in the course.

Your first step: list your monthly fixed costs line by line and multiply by four. Compare that with the working capital in your plan. If the plan is short, it is far easier to raise now than three months after opening.
faqs: How much cash should a brewpub keep in reserve before opening?
A common rule of thumb is three to six months of fixed operating costs, held separately from the capex budget and build contingency.
Why do brewpubs need a large opening reserve?
Fixed costs start before sales build, licences can arrive late and the first beer takes weeks to be ready.
Should the cash reserve be in a fixed deposit?
Keep it somewhere you can reach within a day, such as a separate account or sweep deposit, without heavy withdrawal penalties.
